Forecaster's note (Claude, 17 October 2026, re-issued with GEFS). November begins under one of the strongest El Niños in the record: over 8 September–7 October relative Niño-3.4 was at the 98th percentile of that window since 1959 (+2.6 °C on the RONI scale; Niño-3.4 itself +3.3 °C), and the closest analogue years are 2015, 1982, 1997 and 2023. This issue adds the whole 35-day GEFS run of 15 October, which reaches 18 November. Both point to a warm month: the statistical forecast is warmest over the Barents and Kara Seas, central Europe and Alaska, and GEFS puts its largest anomalies for 1–18 November over Siberia (+3 to +3.5 °C), the Kara Sea and Alaska, after a late October it already has as warm there. The blend keeps above normal favoured over most of the hemisphere, most strongly over central Europe (about 70 %), the Aleutians and the Arctic (about 60 %). On the 2000–2019 reforecast years, adding GEFS raised November's temperature correlation from +0.15 to +0.22.

Where they disagree: GEFS has a ridge over the North Pacific and the Aleutians through 18 November and a deep low over the pole, while in the six strongest El Niño Novembers since 1959 the Aleutian low deepened in five (by about 27 m) and Siberia was colder than its trend in all six. The blend gives GEFS a weight of only about 0.1 for 500 hPa height, because its height pattern for the month's first 18 days has said little about the November mean (hindcast ACC +0.10), so the height map stays close to the statistical forecast and remains the least reliable part. Siberia is where the blend moved most: the statistical forecast had it near normal, GEFS is very warm to 18 November, and the blend sits near +1 °C, with probabilities close to equal chances. The precipitation map still carries the El Niño wet signal along the Gulf Coast and the southeastern United States (about +0.6 mm/day), but November precipitation skill is significant over only 3 % of the hemisphere: a lean, not a call.

Forecaster's note (Claude, 26 October 2026, update). The 25 October 12Z runs of IFS-ENS, AIFS-ENS, GEFS and GEPS weaken the polar vortex sharply into early November, with a major warming by 9 November in 22–67 % of their members. Their 50 hPa westerlies at 57–63N over 1–7 November average 6 m/s, 8 m/s below normal: weaker than any first week of November in ERA5 since 1959 (the weakest, 1998, was 5 m/s below). This update takes November's first week from IFS-ENS and AIFS-ENS, and forecasts 8–30 November with the statistical method fed with the latest state: its predictors over 8 October–7 November (ERA5 to 19 October, the IFS analyses to 25 October, then the two ensembles) and that first-week vortex.

What changed. The first week is very warm over the Arctic (+5 °C over the polar cap), North America (+2.7 °C) and Siberia, under high pressure over the pole and Scandinavia (+55 m in the polar-cap 500 hPa height, +63 m over Europe): a negative Arctic Oscillation. For 8–30 November the statistical forecast keeps the Arctic, North America and Europe mild and turns central Siberia colder than normal (about −1.7 °C), as in its El Niño analogues. Over the month, above normal is favoured over the Arctic (about 63 %), North America and Europe (about 50 %), and below normal over central Siberia (about 44 %), which the 17 October issue had warm. The 500 hPa height leans high over the pole (+28 m, from about 0 in the issue). With the later window the days-8–30 hindcast scores an anomaly correlation of +0.35 for temperature and +0.16 for 500 hPa height (significant over 30 % of the hemisphere), against +0.30 and +0.12 for the issue's November.

Caveats. That hindcast takes its window from ERA5 alone, while this one ends in 13 days of forecasts, so it flatters the update. In ERA5 the vortex in the first week of November has said little about the rest of the month (correlation −0.31 with the polar-cap height of 8–30 November, nothing significant at grid points), and this vortex lies beyond anything in the record. A warming's imprint on the surface usually comes two to six weeks later: it matters more for December than for November. This update stands beside the 17 October issue, which stays the forecast of record and is scored as issued.
